newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. envoy holds Afghan ceasefire talks.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy holds Afghan ceasefire talks.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl brought together leaders of Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban militia and a northern opposition alliance for ceasefire talks at his office in Islamabad on Thursday.

Holl told a news conference that the meeting between the Taleban's acting Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammed Ghous and General Paynda (one name), speaking for the opposition axis, had been "good", but had not produced any immediate result.
Paynda is a member of northern Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli faction.
"It was not an easy meeting," Holl said, adding he expected to bring the two sides together again after a meeting on Afghanistan at the United Nations in New York on November 18.
The Taleban, who seized Kabul on September 27, are battling the forces of ousted government commander Ahmad Shah Masood and Dostum north of the capital and in a northwestern province.
Previous efforts to negotiate a ceasefire, which would include arrangements for an exchange of prisoners and bodies, have foundered on differences over what should happen next.
Holl said both sides had accepted that there should be a political process likely to focus on demilitarising Kabul and handing the battered city over to a neutral force.
But he said they were still far apart on how far the rival forces should pull back from the capital and what the composition of the neutral security force should be.
"We are now in a bargaining phase," he said. "Each side is putting forward maximal positions...There are indications we can bring them together or at closer than they were before."
He played down one major obstacle to an agreement -- the Taleban's demand that their strict version of Islamic Sharia law should be imposed throughout the country.
Holl said attempting to resolve that issue right away might make it impossible to bring about an urgently-needed ceasefire.
The Taleban's acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi indicated in Kabul on Monday that there would be no compromise on the movement's goal of spreading Sharia all over Afghanistan.
"We are ready to negotiate with anybody who accepts our principles," he said after rejecting a reported offer from Dostum of ceasefire talks to be held in the north.

"Dostum has a bad record," he said. "We who call ourselves mujahideen (holy warriors) and Taleban consider our participation in any sort of meeting which is supposed to be headed by Dostum as an insult to Islam and to ourselves."
Ghous met Dostum in the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif last month in abortive peace talks brokered by Pakistan's former interior minister Naseerullah Babar.
Holl said he was in touch with all key Afghan factions and planned to meet Masood very soon for what would be his first face-to-face contact with the renowned guerrilla chief.
